content: Butternut canker, caused by the fungal pathogen Sirococcus clavigignentijuglandacearum (Nair et al., 1979), is a disease that specifically affects members of the family Juglandaceae. Distribution The disease was first identified in Wisconsin in 1967 and has since spread to other states. Surveys have shown that 84% of butternut trees in Michigan and 58% of those in Wisconsin were affected. Later studies revealed that 91% of all living butternut trees were either diseased or had cankers. The disease has also been reported in Canada. Symptoms The disease manifests as elongated and broad cankers on the main stem, branches, young twigs, and exposed roots of the tree. In advanced stages, these cankers are often covered with bark cracks and shredded bark. Life Cycle The fungus releases pycnidiospores during rainy periods. These spores germinate upon contact with wounds or broken branches, penetrating deeply into the tree to form cankers. The infection hyphae typically invade the parenchyma phloem intracellularly but can also penetrate intercellularly through uniand multicellular xylem ray cells and parenchyma cells. Over time, the fungus produces mycelial mats of stroma and mycelial pegs. The stroma generates unior multilocular pycnidia, which contain branched and unbranched conidiophores with two-celled pycnidiospores. These spores are eventually ejected from the pycnidial ostiole. Additionally, the stroma forms interwoven mycelial pegs that exert pressure on the outer periderm of the host bark, exposing the pycnidia beneath. These pegs also produce smaller pycnidia compared to those in the stroma, but the spores they generate are identical. Resistance Different tree species exhibit varying levels of resistance to the fungus. Heartnut and Japanese walnut trees show the highest resistance due to their thick periderm layers (35–45 cells thick), which act as a barrier to pathogen penetration. These trees also produce phenolic compounds immediately upon fungal attack, followed by the production of gums and tyloses to encapsulate the pathogen. Control Breeding for resistance is a critical strategy in managing butternut canker. While the traditional approach has been to remove infected trees to prevent further spread, this practice is increasingly questioned. The disease is now widespread across the butternut range, and removing infected but not dying trees—those that are partially resistant—may eliminate the potential for increased resistance in future generations. There are documented cases of long-term survival of pure butternut trees infected with the canker. Recent findings indicate that the fungus can be internally seed-borne, necessitating strict quarantine protocols for seeds, especially if they are intended for planting in areas where the disease is not yet established.
